translations.text: Jesus went into a city that is called Nain, and so on.
Our Lord went to a certain city called Nain, together with his disciples and a great crowd. When he came near the town gate, a young man's body was being carried out for burial, and so on.
Bede the commentator said that the city of Nain is interpreted as 'wave' or 'commotion.'
The dead young man, who was carried out in the sight of many people, signifies every sinful person who is killed in the inner man by grave sins, and whose wickedness is known to people.
The young man was his mother's only son. In the same way, every Christian is spiritually the son of the holy Church, which is the mother of us all, and yet an undefiled virgin,
because her offspring is not bodily but spiritual. Every servant of God is called a child when he is learning;
but when he teaches another, he is a mother, just as the apostle Paul said about those who had fallen away: "You are my children, whom I now conceive a second time, until Christ is renewed in you."
The town gate signifies one of the bodily senses through which people sin.
The man who sows discord among Christians, or who speaks iniquity on high through the gate of his mouth, is carried out dead.
He who looks at a woman with a lecherous gaze and foul lust, through the gate of his eyes, shows that his soul is dead.
Whoever gladly listens to idle talk or slanderous words makes his ear a gate of death for himself. The same is to be understood of the other senses.
The Saviour was moved with compassion for the mother, to give us an example of his kindness; and afterwards he raised the dead man, to strengthen us in faith in him.
He came near and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. The bier that carried the dead man is the untroubled conscience of the sinner who has no hope.
Truly, the bearers who carried him to burial are the flatteries of fawning companions, who with flattery and poisoned sweet words urge on and praise the sinner, just as the prophet said:
"The sinner is praised in his desires, and the unrighteous man is blessed." When he is surrounded by empty fame and flattery, it is as if he were buried under a heap of earth.
About such people the Saviour spoke to one of his chosen followers, when that man wanted to bury his father's body. He said, "Let the dead bury their dead; you go and proclaim the kingdom of God."
Truly, the dead bury other dead when sinful people flatter others like themselves with harmful praise and crush them under the piled-up weight of the worst flattery.
About such people it is said in another place, "The tongues of flatterers bind people's souls in sins."
When the Lord touched the bier, the bearers stood still. In the same way, if the sinner's conscience is touched with fear of the judgment on high,
then he resists sinful desires and lying flatterers, and promptly answers the Lord who calls him to eternal life, as if he rose from death.
The Lord said to the young man, "I say to you, arise." And he immediately sat up and spoke, and the Saviour gave him to his mother.
The revived man sits up when the sinner comes back to life through divine compunction. He speaks when he occupies his mouth with praises of God and seeks God's mercy through true confession.
He is handed over to his mother when, through the authority of priests, he is joined to the fellowship of the holy Church. The people were struck with great fear;
For just as a person turns from greater sins to God's mercy and corrects his conduct according to God's commandments, so more people are turned to the praise of God through his example.
the Almighty Son of the Almighty Father, who visited his people through his human nature and set them free from slavery to the devil.
We read in many places in books that the Saviour raised many dead people to life, but no gospel account is given of any of them except three only.
One is this young man of whom we have just spoken. The second was the daughter of a ruler. The third was Lazarus, the brother of Martha and Mary.
The rising of these three people signifies the threefold rising of sinful souls.
The death of the soul is of three kinds: the first is evil consent, the second is evil deed, and the third is evil habit.
Christ raises such sinners if they repent of their sins, and he hands them over to their mother; that is, he joins them to the unity of his Church.
The Saviour showed this when he raised the girl with a gentle voice in the sight of a few people;
he raised the young man in the sight of all the people and strengthened him with these words: "Young man, I say to you, arise."
No sin is so great that a person cannot atone for it, if with an inward heart he perseveres in true penance in proportion to the measure of the guilt.

"Though someone speaks a slanderous word against me, it will be forgiven him if he does penance. But truly, whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this world or in the world to come."
The Holy Spirit is truly shared in common by the Father and the Son, because he is the Spirit of them both, that is, the Love and Will of them both, through whom sins are forgiven.
They cannot be named all together at once, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, but they are never separated from one another anywhere for any space of time.
He speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit who, with an unrepentant heart, persists in wicked deeds and scorns the forgiveness that rests on the gift of the Holy Spirit:
